title: Design a Parking Lot (OOD)
oneLiner: The classic "design the classes" round, stage by stage: use cases, classes, a class diagram, C# for the key methods, and the follow-ups.
keyTakeaway: An OOD round is graded on clean responsibilities and on how well the design takes a new requirement, not on how many patterns you name. For the parking lot: a spot that enforces its own rules, assignment and pricing as swappable policies, one lock around "find and take a spot", a ticket status (Active, PaymentPending, Closed) so only one exit can charge a ticket while the card call runs outside the lock, and no Singleton.
explanation:
This is a practice run of an object-oriented design interview, also called low-level design or a "design the classes for X" round. Amazon, Microsoft, Uber and many others use it, often in place of or next to a system design round. The widget plays the interviewer: it gives you the prompt and walks through seven stages. In each one, write your own answer first, then press "Compare with the model answer" and tick the points you really covered. Notes stay in this browser.

How it differs from system design. A system design round is about many machines: load balancers, databases, caches, queues, and the numbers that size them. An OOD round is about one program: which classes exist, what each is responsible for, how they relate, and what the important methods look like in code. Nobody asks for requests per second. Instead you're expected to write real signatures and the body of the one or two methods that hold the hard logic, in the language you'd use on the job (C# here).

The usual flow, about 45 minutes: 5 on requirements and use cases (actors, what's in and out), 5 on the core objects (nouns to classes, one responsibility each), 6 on relationships (a class diagram with inheritance, composition and multiplicity), 10 on key interfaces and methods (C#), 7 on patterns and trade-offs, 6 walking one use case through your methods, and 6 on extensions, where the interviewer adds a requirement and watches how much of your design has to change.

What's graded, roughly in order. Clarifying scope: asking before designing, and saying what you're leaving out. Clean responsibilities: each class does one job you can say in a sentence, with no god class called Manager doing everything. Sensible use of interfaces and composition: an interface where a policy might change (how spots are assigned, how fees are priced), composition over deep inheritance, and inheritance only where there's a real is-a with different behaviour. SOLID without dogma: the principles should show up in the design, not as a lecture, and "I didn't add an interface here because nothing varies" is a good answer. Extensibility: when the interviewer says "now add electric vehicle charging", a good design takes a new class and a small edit. And code: correct, idiomatic signatures and the bodies of the key methods, including concurrency where two callers can race.

The parking lot is the most common OOD question because it looks easy. The depth is in a few places: whether vehicle and spot types need classes or just enums (a type with a fixed list of named values), where the "does this vehicle fit" rule lives, keeping assignment and pricing out of the gate code, making sure two entry gates can't hand out the same spot, not holding a lock while a card terminal is thinking, and making sure two exits can't both charge the same ticket once that lock has been let go.
